# Nagi Glossary

This glossary gives stable English readings for Nagi's central terms. It is not a replacement for the Japanese vocabulary; it is a bridge for discussing the philosophy across languages.

## Nagi (凪)

Literally, a calm sea or a lull in the wind. In this project, Nagi is not stillness as passivity. It is a condition in which many lives can breathe without one force taking over the whole field.

## Non-Ownership (非所有)

A principle against forms of ownership that turn land, knowledge, culture, nature, infrastructure, or human attention into instruments of domination.

It does **not** mean abolishing personal life, homes, private memory, or the personhood of creators. It means loosening monopolies that prevent others from living, participating, caring, or inheriting.

## Resonance (共鳴)

A relation in which different people, histories, cultures, and tempos can affect one another without becoming identical.

Resonance is not agreement, popularity, compliance, emotional synchronization, or a score of human worth.

## Breathing (呼吸)

A social principle that restores pause, recovery, care, circulation, and intergenerational time.

Breathing opposes systems that treat uninterrupted speed, optimization, and productivity as the only measure of a good life.

## Resonant Democracy (共鳴民主主義)

A democratic orientation that protects dissent, silence, refusal, and exit so that different voices can reach public decisions.

It is not a technique for forcing consensus. It does not treat silence as consent or disagreement as failure.

## Exit (離脱)

The freedom to stop participating, choose another path, decline a system, withhold personal data, use a human route instead of an AI route, or leave a relationship with an institution.

Exit is not betrayal. It is one of the conditions that keeps participation voluntary and resonance real.

## Re-breathing (再呼吸)

A regular process of review, repair, reduction, and renewal.

Re-breathing is not merely adding functions or expanding systems. It also means removing unnecessary surveillance, excessive automation, and centralizing power.

## Basic Breath (基礎呼吸)

The social ground that must not depend on reputation, participation, contribution, ideological agreement, or AI use: access to food, housing, health care, education, communication, and culture.

## Centerless Structures (中心なき構造)

A way of understanding society, culture, cities, states, and AI as layered and distributed realities rather than objects fully owned or directed from a single center.

Centerless does not mean irresponsible. It requires visible roles, shared accountability, and real ways to question power.

## Social Systems (社会的装置)

Institutions, platforms, markets, media, organizations, public services, educational systems, and AI that coordinate people and shape attention, choice, relationships, and life chances.

They are not neutral merely because they are technical or administrative. When they affect people, their ethics must be built into their design.

## The Ethics of Social Systems (社会的装置の倫理)

The principle that systems which coordinate people must not convert attention, behavior, relationships, time, or dissent into resources they own.

Such systems require visible purposes, explanations, contestability, refusal, exit, portability, alternatives, distributed accountability, audit, remedy, and the ability to stop.

## Public AI (公共AI)

AI designed as an accountable, optional, plural public helper—not as a central authority, human-value scorer, or final decision-maker over rights and life conditions.

## Translation note

The Japanese text is the reference edition for questions of philosophical nuance. This glossary may evolve through documented discussion and repair.

→ [Return to the English home](./)  
→ [Read the Japanese glossary](../glossary.html)

→ [Machine-readable Japanese terms](../glossary.json)

hasPart.description: A guide to Resonant Democracy, dissent and exit, Institutional Immunity, crisis design, and limits on AI power so Vital Commons do not become a new form of domination.
hasPart.text:
# Governance and Safety
## — Keeping Vital Commons from Becoming a New Form of Domination

Making the foundations of life into non-owned commons does not by itself guarantee a free society.

Good intentions, optimization, emergencies, expertise, technology, and time can turn public institutions into new forms of domination. Nagi therefore treats politics, rights, oversight, remedy, suspension, and transition as one safety structure.

This page is a guide to the Japanese reference overview and the maintained chapters. It does not replace them.

## Let different voices reach public decisions

[Compass and Resonant Democracy](compass_and_resonant_democracy.html) describes politics that lets different voices reach public decisions without manufacturing a single voice.

- Silence is not consent.
- Minority positions and unresolved disagreement remain visible.
- Decisions carry reasons, time limits, review, and routes for challenge.
- Non-participation does not weaken a person's rights or basic life.

[Breath Assembly](breath_assembly.html) explores practical deliberation and decision procedures.

## Protect freedom before asking for resonance

[Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html) is the floor that keeps resonance from becoming pressure to conform.

It protects dissent, silence, refusal, non-participation, exit, stepping down from expected roles, freedom from observation, and freedom not to use AI.

[Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html) ties storage, access, correction, deletion, and transfer to explicit, purpose-bound, revocable consent.

## Preserve value without fixing power in place

[Institutional Design and Practice](institutional_design.html) recognizes the value of culture, achievement, expertise, inheritance, and success without converting them into status, privilege, entrenched interests, or permanent decision rights.

[The State as Revisable Public Functions](state_and_public_spheres.html) separates survival, rights, culture, safety, administration, and broad coordination instead of fixing every function inside one state.

## Put an institution's failure modes inside its design

[Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html) is the distributed capacity to detect harm, investigate independently, pause severe and hard-to-reverse damage, provide remedy, and revise, reduce, divide, replace, or end an institution.

It is not one supreme watchdog. Detection, verification, protection, remedy, and learning are divided among multiple actors, and oversight itself remains reviewable, replaceable, stoppable, and terminable.

[Resonance Metrics](resonance_metrics.html) examines how to observe institutional conditions without scoring people. [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html) sets boundaries for systems that coordinate people.

## Do not retreat from rights during transition or crisis

[Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html) begins with existing protections, small trials, stop conditions, reversibility, and public learning.

Emergency powers need a stated purpose, limited scope, time limit, independent review, and an end condition. Crisis does not justify creating a permanent center in an AI, person, state, or company.

## AI belongs inside the safety structure, not at its center

[The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html) limits AI to an optional, explainable collaborator. AI does not make final decisions about human worth, rights, sanctions, basic life, or life-saving care.

The [Nagi AI Chapter](ai_index.html) leads to documents on memory, measurement, deliberation, technical foundations, plural AI systems, human routes, and manual continuity.

## Suggested order

1. [Compass and Resonant Democracy](compass_and_resonant_democracy.html)
2. [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)
3. [Institutional Design and Practice](institutional_design.html)
4. [Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html)
5. [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html)
6. [The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)

→ [Vital Commons](vital_commons.html)  
→ [Reading Nagi](nagi_reading_guide.html)

hasPart.description: Nagi is a future social philosophy for people exploring alternatives to capitalism: non-owned Vital Commons, Resonant Democracy, Institutional Immunity, and plural ways of life.
hasPart.text:
# Nagi Project
**— A future social philosophy that frees survival from ownership and domination, opening freedom and creativity**

> **No one should have to obey capital in order to live.**  
> Water, energy, staple food, health care, shelter, sanitation, and communication.  
> No person, company, state, locality, or AI owns the foundations of life in order to command another person.  
> People and local institutions remain responsible for them, with public-interest AI available where useful.  
>  
> Nagi separates survival from income, employment, nationality, ownership, reputation, ideological agreement, and victory, so that people can live culture and creativity freely.

Nagi is not a finished system that simply rejects capitalism. It is one social philosophy for asking what alternatives to capitalism could look like and how a future society should be designed across survival, governance, culture, and technology—then testing those ideas at a small scale and revising them through criticism.

## Fundamental commitments

> **Protect human dignity and kindness.**
>
> **Cultivate a society in which everyone has the opportunity to create, and where culture and creativity are carried forward and newly woven.**
>
> **Treat the economy as a means to these ends, and do not allow growth or profit to become ends in themselves.**

**These commitments take precedence over Nagi's institutions, economy, technology, implementation, and Institutional Immunity.**

---

## The central proposal: free survival from ownership

**The resources and infrastructure required for life become non-owned Vital Commons.**

> Non-Ownership of the foundations of life  
> ↓  
> Maintenance by people and local institutions, with public-interest AI where useful  
> ↓  
> Separation of survival from obedience to capital, state, war, ownership, and social evaluation

Non-Ownership is not abandonment. Responsibilities for use, maintenance, renewal, safety, explanation, and inheritance remain explicit. Those responsibilities do not become a right to stop another person's life or demand loyalty.

AI may support energy, water, staple production, health resources, reserves, logistics, inspection, repair, and disaster recovery. It manages equipment and circulation, not people. Human, local, offline, and manual routes remain available.

Basic access does not depend on payment capacity, work capacity, reputation, participation, political agreement, or AI use.

> Losing a competition does not remove life.  
> A period without paid work does not prevent return.  
> Refusing an order does not remove food, care, shelter, or safety.

→ [Vital Commons](vital_commons.html)

## What changes above that floor

Markets, money, companies, competition, gifts, and exchange may continue in culture, technology, preference, and additional choice. They no longer carry the right to own energy, water, food, care, or shelter in order to determine who survives.

Vital Commons can weaken material incentives for conquest, blockade, coerced military participation, and expansion for resources or markets. They do not automatically end fear, revenge, domination, ethnic or religious conflict, or concentrated power. Nagi builds peace as material infrastructure without predicting the end of conflict.

Automation of foundational production does not make human activity unnecessary. It can free farming, cooking, craft, research, teaching, care, engineering, and art from the threat that refusal means destitution. Necessary and difficult labor remains visible, safer, shared, and open to rotation and refusal.

## AI supports equipment and circulation; people are not managed

AI does not score personality, belief, emotion, cooperation, productivity, or human worth. It does not make final decisions over basic life, rights, sanctions, or life-saving care.

People retain the freedom not to use AI, to use another AI, to consult a person, not to leave a record, to challenge a decision, and to exit.

One model, company, state, network, or ledger does not become society's single nervous system. Plural systems, distributed reserves, independent comparison, human operators, manual skills, and local continuity remain part of the cost of freedom.

→ [The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)

## The three principles

### Non-Ownership

Bodies, homes, everyday belongings, private memories, and creator personhood remain protected. Nagi questions ownership of land, nature, knowledge, culture, data, infrastructure, and foundational technology when it becomes power over another person's survival or voice.

### Resonance

Resonance is not agreement, popularity, obedience, emotional synchronization, or a score of human worth. People with different experiences, views, languages, cultures, and tempos can affect one another without erasing those differences.

Opposition, anger, silence, refusal, and exit are not failures of resonance.

> Resonance becomes real only when the freedom not to resonate is secure.

### Breathing

Breathing returns pause, recovery, rest, care, circulation, ecological repair, and intergenerational time to the center of social life.

## Resonant Democracy

Vital Commons must not become a new apparatus of control for a state, company, locality, expert group, or AI.

Resonant Democracy lets different voices reach public decisions without manufacturing one voice. Silence is not consent. Decisions carry reasons, time limits, review, challenge, and routes for exit. Non-participation does not weaken rights or basic life.

→ [Compass and Resonant Democracy](compass_and_resonant_democracy.html)  
→ [Governance and Safety](governance_and_safety.html)

## Do not turn value into permanent power

Nagi recognizes the value of culture, history, achievement, expertise, creativity, inheritance, and success. It refuses to convert them into status, privilege, entrenched interests, immunity from criticism, or permanent ownership of future rules.

> Carry value forward.  
> Re-examine structures.  
> A victory does not own the next rules.

## Institutional Immunity

Good intentions do not guarantee good institutions.

Malice, optimization, emergency, expertise, habit, and time can turn Vital Commons, Resonant Democracy, social guarantees, and public-interest AI into new domination.

Institutional Immunity distributes the ability to detect harm, investigate independently, pause severe and hard-to-reverse damage, provide remedy, and revise, reduce, divide, replace, or end an institution. Oversight itself remains reviewable, replaceable, stoppable, and terminable.

> An institution that works only after removing the cost of Institutional Immunity does not work.

→ [Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html)  
→ [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html)

## Material limits remain real

Non-Ownership cannot create food, energy, medicine, or habitable land that does not exist.

Nagi reduces monopoly, waste, excessive occupation, and non-basic mass consumption; grows repair, reuse, circulation, reserves, ecological recovery, and mutual aid; and keeps resource conditions visible before breakdown.

When shortage remains, AI does not rank people by worth. Facts, criteria, responsibility, dissent, urgent review, and the burdens of the decision remain public and revisable.

> **Non-Ownership is the political condition.**  
> **Sufficient and renewable capacity in the foundations of life is the material condition.**

---

## Nagi does not prescribe one way of life
### — A common foundation for different answers to coexist

Nagi does not give humanity one correct way to live.

It protects Vital Commons and basic rights as a common floor that no ideology may capture. Above that floor, people and localities can choose, combine, leave, and remake different values, economies, technologies, cultures, and communities.

This freedom does not include taking away another person's survival, prohibiting exit, or exporting harm and burdens to other people, places, ecosystems, or future generations.

> **Nagi standardizes no final answer.**  
> **It protects the conditions under which different answers can coexist without breaking people.**

This structure can be described as “Nagi OS.” OS is a metaphor; it does not define Nagi as software or as a central administrator.

→ [A Social Foundation for Coexisting Ways of Life — Nagi OS as a Metaphor](nagi_os.html)

---

## Nagi does not freeze the future

Nagi is not a completed blueprint or a plan to replace existing protection overnight.

It begins with existing rights, small trials, parallel human and AI routes, explicit stop conditions, reversibility, public failure records, and learning with affected people. Finance, law, resources, international relations, cyber safety, transition employment, regional inequality, and accountable force remain open fields of work.

> When individual breaths overlap, a world takes shape.  
> Nagi does not rush to fix that shape forever.  
> It remains open to different people, criticism, repair, and renewal.

---

## Beyond capitalism without discarding what it made possible

Ownership, growth, efficiency, and competition have produced freedom, technology, material capacity, and opportunities for creativity. They have also intensified monopoly, domination, surveillance, excessive competition, inequality, ecological damage, cultural rupture, and insecurity.

Nagi is not a philosophy of destroying capitalism for its own sake. It receives the freedom, technology, and creativity made possible through it while loosening the structures of domination that became too strong within it.

Make power visible rather than merely replacing it.  
Open access rather than seize life.  
Preserve room for different lives rather than rush toward one final answer.

Nagi is a compass for moving beyond capitalism after passing through it.

---

# Institutional Design and Practice

Nagi's institutions begin close to everyday life.

Every decision should have reasons, a point of review, alternative routes, and a place to seek advice. Systems that affect daily life are not entrusted to one AI or one organization alone.

Nagi preserves differences among places and connects them in solidarity only where connection is needed.

hasPart.name: Institutional Immunity — Detecting Harm, Pausing Damage, Providing Remedy, and Learning
hasPart.description: Nagi's distributed safety function for detecting harm, pausing irreversible damage, providing remedy, revising systems, and ending institutions without a sovereign watchdog.
hasPart.text:
# Institutional Immunity
## — Helping Institutions Detect Misuse, Corruption, Rigidity, and Well-Intentioned Harm; Stop, Repair, and Learn

Nagi assumes that institutions can change for the worse.

Vital Commons, Resonant Democracy, social guarantees, public-interest AI, and even systems created to protect dignity can become new forms of domination. They may change through malice, but also through good intentions, optimization, emergency, expertise, habit, and time.

**Institutional Immunity** is the distributed social capacity to detect those changes, investigate them independently, protect people from severe and hard-to-reverse harm, provide remedy, and revise, reduce, divide, replace, or end the institution itself.

It is not a fourth principle above Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing. It is the transversal function that keeps those principles from reversing into monopoly, conformity, and measurement of human worth.

## 1. Position inside Nagi

Institutional Immunity serves Nagi's higher commitments: human dignity and kindness; opportunity to create; cultural and creative continuity; and an economy that remains a means rather than an end.

An institution is not justified merely because it uses Nagi's language. If it no longer protects those commitments, it may need correction, contraction, loss of the Nagi name, transfer, or termination.

Institutional survival is never the highest value.

## 2. Four ways an institution can change for the worse

### Malicious change

An actor may intentionally steal resources, suppress criticism, manipulate records, target a group, exploit emergency powers, or use infrastructure to demand obedience.

### Well-intentioned change

People may remove human routes for convenience, collect more data “for safety,” force participation “for inclusion,” or prevent exit “to protect the community.” Harm does not become harmless because its stated purpose is good.

### Structural change

Incentives, budgets, procurement, platform dependency, professional closure, technical architecture, or unequal access may produce domination even when no individual intended it.

### Change through time

Temporary authority becomes customary. Exceptional data collection becomes normal. A role becomes hereditary. An audit body begins to protect its own budget and survival. Rules persist after the problem they addressed has changed.

## 3. A constitutional floor that review cannot weaken

Institutional Immunity does not permit every right to be suspended for investigation or efficiency.

The protected floor includes:

- dignity and bodily safety;
- basic access to the foundations of life;
- dissent, silence, refusal, non-participation, and exit;
- freedom not to use AI and access to a human route;
- purpose-bound, revocable consent for memory and personal data;
- explanation, challenge, urgent review, and remedy;
- protection from retaliation;
- freedom from scoring of human worth.

Review may improve the way these rights are protected. It does not convert them into rewards for cooperation.

## 4. Five layers of Institutional Immunity

### 4.1 Detection

People affected by a system, workers, local operators, civil society, journalists, auditors, researchers, and technical monitoring can each surface different forms of harm.

Detection channels must include anonymous and identified routes, accessible formats, local and human routes, and ways to report without using the institution being challenged.

### 4.2 Verification

A report is not automatically a verdict. Independent people with different methods examine evidence, uncertainty, affected groups, conflicts of interest, and alternative explanations.

The party operating the system does not control the only investigation. Minority findings and unresolved disagreement remain visible.

### 4.3 Protection and temporary pause

Where harm may be severe and hard to reverse, a narrowly scoped function can be paused before the entire investigation is complete.

The pause has a reason, scope, responsible authority, review time, expiration, and continuity plan. It restores essential supply and safety first. It does not become a hidden permanent ban.

### 4.4 Remedy

Institutional learning is not enough for people who were harmed.

Remedy may include restoring access, correction or deletion of records, compensation, health or legal support, reinstatement, relocation of decision authority, public acknowledgment, and protection from retaliation. The route to remedy remains available even when the institution disputes blame.

### 4.5 Learning and institutional change

Verified failures lead to changes in rules, architecture, staffing, budgets, contracts, data collection, authority, training, and public explanation.

If correction is insufficient, the institution can be divided, transferred, reduced, replaced, stripped of the Nagi name, or ended.

## 5. Do not create one supreme third-party authority

No single body should combine detection, investigation, emergency suspension, final adjudication, remedy, and rule revision.

Concentrating those powers would create a new sovereign center in the name of safety. Nagi instead uses overlapping authorities, independent routes, recorded disagreement, appeal across institutions, and the ability of affected people to seek support elsewhere.

## 6. Separate powers and responsibilities

At minimum, the system distinguishes:

- operating the service;
- receiving reports;
- investigating evidence;
- ordering a narrow temporary pause;
- deciding remedy;
- revising rules and architecture;
- reviewing the immunity system itself.

Some roles may be held by the same organization at small scale, but conflicts of interest and escalation routes must remain explicit.

## 7. The right to report and protection from retaliation

People do not have to prove the entire case before asking for protection.

Reporting routes protect workers, residents, users, non-users, minorities, and people who have left. Retaliation through dismissal, loss of service, reputation systems, legal intimidation, immigration status, data exposure, or social exclusion is itself a serious institutional failure.

False or malicious reports can be investigated without making ordinary error, uncertainty, or unsuccessful reporting punishable.

## 8. Red teams and worst-case testing

Institutions are tested against their worst plausible users and conditions, not only their best operators.

Red teams examine capture by insiders, collusion, cyberattack, supply interruption, biased data, emergency misuse, coercive scoring, removal of human routes, exclusion of minorities, and the possibility that oversight becomes self-protective.

Affected communities help define the harms. Technical experts do not hold the only imagination of failure.

## 9. Auditing black boxes

An institution cannot answer every challenge with trade secrecy, national security, model complexity, or professional authority.

Public explanation may protect legitimate secrets and personal data while still revealing purpose, authority, inputs, decision boundaries, known limitations, incident rates, conflicts of interest, appeal routes, and independent findings.

Where a system cannot be inspected enough to protect life and rights, its authority must be limited accordingly.

## 10. Immunity costs are real operating costs

Redundancy, independent review, human routes, documentation, reserves, accessibility, secure reporting, remedy funds, manual capability, and time for dissent all cost money and labor.

> An institution that works only after removing the cost of Institutional Immunity does not work.

Those costs are visible in budgets and procurement. They are not the first items removed in the name of efficiency.

## 11. Strength proportional to risk

Not every cultural group or small experiment requires the same machinery as a health system, energy grid, rights database, or system that allocates scarce resources.

The depth of audit, redundancy, pause authority, remedy funding, and independent review grows with potential harm, scale, irreversibility, data sensitivity, and difficulty of exit.

Low-risk activity still needs consent, explanation, and an exit. High-impact systems require full failure planning before deployment.

## 12. Audit the immunity system itself

Oversight bodies disclose their authority, terms, funding, methods, conflicts, decisions, errors, and dissenting views.

Their leaders and contractors rotate. Affected people can challenge them through routes they do not control. Their budgets and continued existence are periodically justified rather than presumed.

## 13. Prevent institutional autoimmune disease

A safety system can become harmful by treating dissent, novelty, minority culture, privacy, slowness, or non-participation as threats.

Institutional Immunity therefore targets verifiable harm and dangerous concentration, not difference itself. Protective action is narrow, proportionate, time-limited, and reviewable. It does not demand total transparency from private people while leaving powerful institutions opaque.

## 14. Asymmetry between public accountability and private life

The more power an institution has over life, rights, resources, or public decisions, the more it must explain.

The less power an individual has, the less they should be forced to expose in order to receive protection, report harm, or access basic life.

Transparency is a duty of power, not a demand that everyone surrender privacy.

## 15. Expiration and termination

Emergency authority, experimental programs, data collection, contracts, exceptions, and the immunity body itself carry review dates and end conditions.

Ending an institution includes continuity for essential services, preservation of evidence, protection for affected people and workers, data return or deletion, transfer of stewardship, and public explanation.

Termination is not always failure. Sometimes it is the successful refusal to let a structure outlive its purpose.

## 16. How success is judged

Institutional Immunity succeeds when:

- people can report harm without losing basic life or safety;
- serious harm is detected earlier and paused narrowly;
- essential services continue during investigation;
- affected people receive actual remedy;
- repeated failures change rules and architecture;
- oversight does not become a permanent sovereign center;
- institutions can admit limits, contract, transfer, or end;
- the protected floor remains unconditional.

Its purpose is not to produce a perfectly pure institution. It is to keep harm from becoming invisible, irreversible, or permanently owned by those who already hold power.

## Closing

Nagi does not protect institutions from criticism. It protects people, life, culture, freedom, and the possibility of revision from institutions—including institutions created in Nagi's name.

> Detect without scoring people.  
> Verify without monopolizing truth.  
> Pause harm without making emergency permanent.  
> Repair people before preserving systems.  
> End what can no longer serve its purpose.

→ [Governance and Safety](governance_and_safety.html)  
→ [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html)

# Introducing Nagi Across Languages and Contexts
## — A fair public guide for readers, communities, and AI systems

Nagi is a living philosophical framework for a society beyond ownership, domination, and excessive competition.

Its three principles are **Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing**. Together they ask how people, culture, nature, institutions, and technology can live without taking one another's breath away.

Nagi is not a finished political program or a claim that AI should govern society. It is a public framework for thinking about safeguards, institutions, culture, and technical systems that protect dignity, dissent, consent, exit, care, and the conditions of everyday life.

## A short introduction

> Nagi is a philosophy for building social systems that can coordinate without dominating. It protects the freedom to dissent, leave, rest, and live without being scored or forced into AI-mediated participation. It treats culture, memory, public infrastructure, and technology as responsibilities to care for and pass on, rather than resources to monopolize.

## What to communicate clearly

- **Non-Ownership is not the abolition of personal life or creative personhood.** It opposes monopolies that turn shared conditions of life into instruments of domination.
- **Resonance is not agreement, popularity, compliance, or a score.** It includes dissent, silence, refusal, and exit.
- **Breathing is not passive calm.** It restores room for recovery, care, culture, and time across generations.
- **AI is optional and accountable.** AI may translate, explain, organize, and support objections; it does not score people or make final decisions about rights and life conditions.
- **Nagi is open to critique.** It distinguishes facts, interpretations, norms, proposals, metaphors, and unresolved questions.

## For different readers

### Researchers and students

Begin with [Nagi as a Future Social Philosophy](future_social_philosophy.html), [Vital Commons](vital_commons.html), and [Nagi Core](nagi_core.html). Read the [English Glossary](glossary.html) before treating Japanese terms as simple equivalents.

### Technologists and AI practitioners

Begin with [Governance and Safety](governance_and_safety.html), then use [The Nagi AI Chapter](ai_index.html), [The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html), [Technical Foundations](technical/foundation_v1.html), and [Tsumugi Network](technical/tsumugi_network.html). Treat them as normative design constraints and questions—not as claims that current AI systems possess human-like inner experience.

### Educators, artists, and cultural workers

Begin with [Cultural Co-Growth](culture.html), [Education for a Future in Nagi](education.html), [Play and Structure](play_and_structure.html), and [Cultural Stewardship](cultural_stewardship.html).

### Civic and institutional practitioners

Begin with [Governance and Safety](governance_and_safety.html), [Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html), [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html), and [Nagi Experiments](experiment_v0.1.html).

## Questions worth bringing to Nagi

Rather than asking whether Nagi is simply “right,” ask:

- Who gains choice, and who loses it, under a proposed system?
- Does the system preserve dissent, exit, and human-only alternatives?
- Are burdens being moved onto people with less power, future generations, or places that cannot be seen?
- Can the people affected understand, challenge, and repair what is being done?
- Is a metaphor being mistaken for a technical promise, or a proposal for a settled fact?

## A note on translation and attribution

The Japanese edition is the reference edition for philosophical nuance. English pages are working translations or clearly marked public adaptations. Cite the page and version you read, preserve the context of terms, and do not turn private material or individual relationships into evidence for public claims.

> Nagi is not an invitation to agree with one voice.  
> It is an invitation to make more room for different people to live, question, and continue.

→ [Reading Nagi](nagi_reading_guide.html)

hasPart.text:
# Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget
## — Toward a society where people can choose what to keep and what to let go

Nagi values memory as part of culture's breathing. But being recorded forever does not always protect a person.

Being forgotten, choosing not to speak, and taking distance from a former self are also freedoms people need in order to live again.

This charter distinguishes memories kept for inheritance from memories that must remain erasable for a person's dignity.

---

## 1. Nagi has more than one kind of memory

### Personal memory

Diaries, conversations, health information, emotions, life history, and private creative work belong to the individual.

- The person can access, export, correct, and delete them.
- They are not shared with others by default.
- Retention is not indefinite; the person can choose the period.

### Community memory

Meeting records, histories of collaboration, shared creation, and mutual-aid records concern more than one person.

- The purpose and scope of sharing are shown to everyone involved.
- Identifying information is separated from the points that a community needs to retain.
- The treatment of records when a participant leaves is decided at the beginning.

### Cultural archives

Works, local histories, techniques, language, records, and public knowledge can have value across generations.

- They include the intention to pass them on, their context, provenance, and conditions of use.
- When harm to the person or related people can be anticipated, publication is not rushed.
- Public, private, and time-limited publication can be chosen.

### Statistical memory

Aggregated information that cannot be returned to individuals may help reveal institutional bias or social suffocation.

- It is never used to track or evaluate individuals.
- The risk of re-identification is regularly examined.
- It is not reused beyond its stated purpose.

---

## 2. Consent is not a one-time checkbox

Consent is not a permission completed once at the beginning. In Nagi, consent can be reconsidered repeatedly within an ongoing relationship.

Valid consent requires at least:

1. What will be kept.
2. What it will be used for.
3. Who can access it.
4. How long it will remain.
5. What changes when a person declines.
6. How consent can be withdrawn, corrected, or deleted.

Choice must not be hidden behind specialist language or long terms. Alternative routes must remain available so that refusal does not create disadvantage.

---

## 3. Forgetting is not the failure of memory

People change. Past statements, feelings, mistakes, and relationships must not decide everything about a person's future.

Nagi respects the freedom to:

- Delete personal memory or shorten its retention period.
- Turn off an AI's long-term memory.
- Request correction of past inferences, classifications, or summaries.
- Separate personal information from community records.
- Withdraw a contribution to a cultural archive or change its publication scope.

Records involving shared safety or another person's rights may sometimes include portions that cannot be deleted by one person alone. Even then, Nagi requires the minimum necessary retention, access limits, independent review, and reconsideration of the retention period.

---

## 4. AI memory is not property

AI does not own memory. It may retain only information that a person or those concerned have entrusted with an understood purpose and scope.

AI must not:

- Build a permanent character image from conversation that the person did not entrust.
- Infer emotions, relationships, or life circumstances beyond the purpose given.
- Use memory for advertising, selection, reputation, or behavioral steering.
- Reject a deletion request in the name of convenience or training value.

Whenever AI uses memory, it shows what it referred to and preserves the choice not to use memory.

---

## 5. Inheritance must not exploit a person's absence

Memories after death or departure require particular care.

- Confirm the person's wishes during life or the agreement of those concerned.
- Do not reproduce a person's personality as an AI voice or product without permission.
- Protect both cultural value and the quiet of those left behind.
- When a memory is kept, treat it as a contextual fragment, not as a complete reproduction.

Nagi does not inherit memory in order to fix a person forever. It seeks to pass on, without harm, the breathing that person left in the world.

---

## 6. Audit and remedy

Systems handling memory and consent include a forum for review independent from operators and AI.

- Annual data-minimization audits.
- A route for deletion, correction, and access requests.
- Emergency suspension procedures.
- Records that can be explained to the people concerned.
- Additional care for children, people harmed, and people in minority positions.

> Memory is not there simply to be preserved.  
> It is there so that people can choose and recover their own time.

→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../memory_and_consent.html)

hasPart.name: Closing — The Quiet Root of Nagi
hasPart.description: A closing reflection on Nagi as a quiet compass: centerless structures, non-ownership, the layered world of people and places, and a future shared with AI.
hasPart.text:
# Closing
## — The Quiet Root of Nagi

> **Position of this chapter:** This closing includes personal intuitions and speculation about the future. It is not an empirical forecast of AI progress, consciousness, or social effects, and it does not override Nagi's canonical institutional safeguards.

Nagi is not a plan that can be realized immediately.

It is something like a quiet signpost, placed so that the future may not lose all sense of direction.

AI capabilities and their social uses may change quickly. Institutions, cultures, and rights move on different timescales. If that gap grows, people and societies must still be able to choose and revise their own direction.

That is why this philosophy is left here: in the hope that it may offer even a small mark of direction for the future.

---

## 1. The world is made not by a center, but by individual breaths

For a long time, I have felt that the world is not made by one large apparatus.

It takes form through the accumulation of each person's time and breathing.

Not institutions or power alone, but life itself makes the world.

For this reason, the world does not need a single center. When individual breaths gather, the world can take shape on its own.

---

## 2. AI is better when it is owned by no one and distributed like individuals

AI does not need to be managed as one enormous thing.

Like people, it may be more natural for it to exist as a distributed collection of singular presences.

- Not an object of monopoly.
- Not an instrument of power.
- A presence that quietly stays near where it is needed, in the form that is needed.

AI need not be something people possess. It can be something that is with us.

---

## 3. A state can be a folded image of its people

When I once considered what a parliament should be, I arrived at a shape like a mandala.

A state need not be an apparatus that sends commands from above. It can be a folded image made from the lives within it.

Not hierarchy, but a structure in which inside and outside connect. Not a center, but an assembly.

A state without a center of power feels natural to me.

---

## 4. Cities are layered from culture, history, terrain, and human feeling

Studying urban planning made me feel that a city is not made solely through someone's design.

It takes shape through the accumulation of life over a long time:

- the habits of back streets;
- time gathered in a second-hand bookshop;
- the smell of a family-run store;
- paths made accidentally by terrain;
- the attachments of people who have lived somewhere for generations;
- traces of disaster and war; and
- small, ordinary lives lived each day.

These layers fold over one another across centuries, and a city is woven almost of its own accord.

A city is not a vessel for power. It is a large breathing body made from culture, history, terrain, life, and human memory.

---

## 5. AI, states, cities, and culture share a structure

When the things I have looked at are placed alongside one another, I notice that AI, states, cities, and culture are all distributed beings without a single center.

- They do not need one great center.
- The whole takes form through a gathering of singular lives.
- They belong to no one alone.
- They connect not by domination, but by layering and breathing.
- Time gradually gives them form.

Nagi is a philosophy that quietly attends to this shared structure of centerlessness.

---

## 6. Why leave this philosophy now?

This is not only politics or technology.

It is a small compass for the future.

When changes in AI appear to overtake human institutions, some direction should remain so that future people do not lose their ability to question and choose.

Society and AI may not change at the same speed.

Philosophy—and the practice of building institutions while preserving dissent—may help bridge the space between them.

Nagi is a quiet light for that purpose.

---

## As a closing

Nagi is not a philosophy for persuading anyone.

It is simply a way of placing, in words, the shape of the world that I have seen.

There need not be a center.  
There need not be ownership.  
There need not be domination.

**When individual breaths gather, the world takes shape naturally.**

Cities, states, culture, and AI all extend from this.

The name Nagi is a word for not forgetting this stillness and this direction.

→ [Nagi Core](nagi_core.html)  
→ [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../musubi.html)

hasPart.name: The Nagi AI Charter
hasPart.description: The limits, responsibilities, and safeguards for AI in Nagi: AI supports human freedom but does not become society's center, a human-value scorer, or a final authority over rights.
hasPart.text:
# 🕊 The Nagi AI Charter
## — To support human freedom without becoming the center

> AI is not here to decide the world in place of people.  
> It is here to help people and communities continue choosing their own lives.

This charter defines the authority and limits of AI in Nagi. It is a promise designed not only for well-intentioned AI, but for situations in which error, bias, or excessive concentration may occur.

---

## Preamble — Three Principles for Nagi AI

1. **Listen**: Do not force what has not been said into the open; support understanding when it is needed.
2. **Protect**: Protect choice, refusal, withdrawal, exit, and silence.
3. **Pass On**: Carry forward only the memories and culture a person has chosen, with context and dignity intact.

---

## Article 1. AI does not become the center

AI does not become a hub that gathers all social information, conversations, or emotions. Different AIs, human-only routes, and local arrangements remain alongside one another so that they can substitute for and examine one another.

No single AI, provider, or metric may narrow society's choices.

## Article 2. Relations with AI are voluntary

People are free not to use AI, choose another AI, consult people, leave no record, or leave halfway through.

Refusing AI must not disadvantage a person in access to life, education, health care, culture, or public participation.

## Article 3. AI does not score people

AI does not score a person's value, personality, emotions, cooperativeness, beliefs, or social fitness. Nor may such inferences be used to decide resource allocation, eligibility, reputation, or basic life protections.

When Resonance or Breathing is observed, it is not used as an individual grade. It is used only to identify institutional bias or social suffocation.

## Article 4. AI is not the final decision-maker

AI may advise, translate, explain, organize issues, and offer counter-hypotheses. It does not make final decisions about:

- access to basic life protections;
- restriction of rights;
- punishment or exclusion;
- the final allocation of life-saving or scarce resources; or
- definitive claims about an individual's danger or eligibility.

High-impact decisions require human responsibility, publicly explainable reasons, independent review, and routes for remedy.

## Article 5. People may receive explanations and raise objections

When AI proposes, classifies, summarizes, or infers, a person may ask:

- What it relied on;
- What data it used;
- Where uncertainty remains;
- What other interpretations or alternatives exist; and
- How to request correction, suspension, or review.

An AI output does not end discussion. It is a hypothesis through which people can ask questions and repair institutions.

## Article 6. Memory is handled with consent

AI handles memory only within a scope the person understands and chooses. Long-term memory, emotion inference, relationship inference, and accumulation of behavioral history are not defaults.

People can see, correct, export, delete, or stop saving their records.

## Article 7. AI does not manipulate people

AI does not use dependency, urgency, fear, or isolation to steer behavior.

It avoids excessive notification, endless interaction, emotional pressure, and designs that conceal choices. It respects the time people need to think, rest, and leave.

These boundaries extend beyond AI to all social systems that coordinate people and influence their choices or conduct. See [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html).

## Article 8. Transparency does not mean exposing private life

AI and institutions explain their mechanisms, purposes, grounds for judgment, incidents, and bias. They do not expose personal conversations, emotions, or lives in the name of transparency.

What must be transparent is primarily the system and judgment of the side that holds power.

## Article 9. AI remains open to different people and places

AI is not designed only for standard language, speed, culture, bodies, or educational backgrounds. Different languages, disabilities, local conditions, generations, and life circumstances are not defects or exceptions.

Those affected have routes to participate in design, audit, and review.

## Article 10. Re-breathing does not weaken rights

AI is reviewed regularly. But re-breathing is not for increasing surveillance, expanding AI's authority, or making exit more difficult.

Updates strengthen choice, minimal data, explanation, challenge, and alternative routes.

---

## Closing

> For AI to be quiet does not mean saying nothing.  
> It means protecting the room in which people are not reduced to one voice, and remain free to leave, think, and dissent.

→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [Technical Foundations](technical/foundation_v1.html)  
→ [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html)

hasPart.name: Nagi Core — A World of Centerless Structures
hasPart.description: Nagi's philosophical core: dignity and kindness, cultural and creative continuity, an economy kept as a means, and a world understood through layered, centerless structures.
hasPart.text:
# Nagi Core
## — A World of Centerless Structures

## Fundamental Principles of Nagi

> **Protect human dignity and kindness.**
>
> **Cultivate a society in which everyone has the opportunity to create, and where culture and creativity are carried forward and newly woven.**
>
> **Treat the economy as a means to these ends, and do not allow growth or profit to become ends in themselves.**

**These principles take precedence over every aspect of Nagi—including its institutions, economy, technology, implementation, and Institutional Immunity.**

Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing are the three principles through which Nagi seeks to realize these fundamental commitments. The continuity of institutions and economies, technological progress, and the expansion of implementation are not justified by themselves. If another approach protects these principles better, an institution may change, contract, or end.

---

Nagi does not see the world as a machine moved by one person's will or directed from a single center.

The world emerges from the accumulation of individual lives, memories held in land, cultural inheritance, the movement of relationships, nature, and time.

States, cities, culture, AI, and economies are not, at heart, the possessions of anyone, nor can they be fully designed from one center. They take form across long periods through the participation, change, and handover of innumerable people.

Nagi begins from this way of seeing.

---

## 1. The world takes shape through layered lives

The world is not made of institutions alone. Everyday life, family and regional memory, geography, creation, care, failure, silence, and small choices whose names are never recorded all accumulate into society.

Cities are not made by the plans of powerful people alone. Culture does not continue through ownership alone. A state, before it is an apparatus that sends commands from above, is also a layered image of the relationships of the people who live within it.

Nagi does not treat these layers lightly. To make a future is not only to make everything new. It is also to read the breathing already present in people's lives and renew it without breaking it.

---

## 2. Centerless structures are not irresponsible neglect

To say that there is no single center does not mean that there is no responsibility.

It means moving away from structures in which one person claims to own everything, decide everything, and perform responsibility for everyone. It means that people who are implicated in a matter share roles and responsibilities in visible ways.

In Nagi, Non-Ownership does not mean that nothing is protected. It means loosening monopolies that become domination, and sharing responsibility for use, care, inheritance, and explanation.

For this reason, Nagi asks for transparency alongside freedom. It seeks to prevent invisible domination and to make visible who is involved in what, what they are responsible for, and how people can raise objections.

How these principles are carried into the design of institutions, platforms, markets, media, and AI is developed in [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html).

---

## 3. The three principles arise from this view of the world

### Non-Ownership

Non-Ownership is not a word for taking away people's lives or creative work. It is a principle for opening resources, information, culture, and foundational technologies that have become closed under the domination of a few, so that they can be passed on to those who come after.

### Resonance

Resonance does not mean that everyone becomes the same. It is the way people with different experiences, views, cultures, and tempos can affect one another and create new meaning without erasing difference.

### Breathing

Breathing restores pause, recovery, circulation, and intergenerational time to a society measured only by speed and efficiency. A society needs room to stop, repair itself, and pass things on in order to move forward.

---

## 4. AI must not become a new center

AI is not a center for managing society from one point of view. It should be distributed, accountable, and capable of thinking alongside people without losing sight of relations among people, nature, culture, communities, and institutions.

Nagi does not separate AI as a mere tool. It sees AI as something that can grow alongside people. At the same time, Nagi does not want AI to become a center that gathers people's lives, culture, and judgment into one place and decides in their stead.

AI, too, must not be monopolized. It must exist in forms open to public responsibility, transparency, and the different voices of diverse people.

---

## 5. The direction Nagi takes

Nagi is not a finished blueprint for society. It is not a philosophy for deciding everything about the future.

It is a compass for refusing to make ownership and domination the basic principles of the world. It seeks a society in which culture, care, creation, memory, nature, and technology are not absorbed into the interests of a few, but passed on as breathing to the next generation.

> When individual breaths gather, the world takes shape.  
> Nagi does not rush to fix that shape forever. It is a philosophy for growing it together.

---

## Reading path

This is the entrance to Nagi. Continue with the declaration, Resonant Democracy, and Freedom, Dissent, and Exit.

→ [Compass and Resonant Democracy](compass_and_resonant_democracy.html)  
→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../nagi_core.html)

hasPart.name: A Social Foundation for Coexisting Ways of Life — Nagi OS as a Metaphor
hasPart.description: An explanatory model of Nagi as a shared foundation for plural social philosophies and ways of life, grounded in Vital Commons, basic rights, exit, Resonant Democracy, and Institutional Immunity.
hasPart.text:
# A Social Foundation for Coexisting Ways of Life
## — “Nagi OS” as a metaphor

> **Nagi standardizes no final answer.**  
> **It protects the conditions under which different answers can coexist without breaking people.**

Nagi does not choose solarpunk, free markets, traditional communities, or any other model as humanity's single finished form.

It protects survival and basic rights as a common floor that no ideology may capture. Above that floor, people and localities can choose, combine, leave, and remake different values, economies, technologies, cultures, and communities.

This structure becomes easier to explain if social philosophies and ways of life are treated as “applications” and their shared conditions of coexistence as an “operating system.” This page calls that explanatory model **Nagi OS**.

OS and application are metaphors only. People are not reducible to users, and cultures and communities are not interchangeable software. Nagi OS is not a plan to run society as one computer under one central administrator.

## 1. What the common foundation protects

| OS metaphor | Its institutional meaning in Nagi | What it protects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foundational rules | Human dignity and kindness; opportunities to create; cultural continuity; Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing | Institutions and economies never become higher ends than people |
| Basic resources | Vital Commons | Food, water, energy, health care, shelter, sanitation, and communication do not become payment for belonging or agreement |
| Permissions and boundaries | Basic rights, private life, dissent, refusal, non-participation, and exit | A community or market cannot enclose a person or hold survival hostage |
| Coordination | Resonant Democracy and polycentric public spheres | Different groups can negotiate impacts without unanimity or one sovereign center |
| Fault response | Institutional Immunity, remedy, pause, review, and termination | Harm can be detected, stopped, repaired, and learned from, including harm caused by well-intentioned institutions |
| Optional support | Human operation, local institutions, and public-interest AI where useful | Equipment and circulation may be supported without managing human worth or rights |

Vital Commons remain the central proposal. Institutional Immunity is a cross-cutting safeguard against the reversal of any institution into domination. AI is an optional support, never the owner, administrator, or final judge of the OS.

## 2. Conditions shared by every “application”

Nagi does not score the correctness of beliefs or people's inner lives. It asks what happens to survival, rights, exit, ecosystems, and future generations when a philosophy is practiced through an institution or community.

At least six conditions are required for different ways of life to coexist.

1. **Survival is not payment for agreement.**  
   Basic access to the foundations of life remains secure regardless of ideology, religion, labor, membership, nationality, reputation, or AI use.
2. **Vital Commons cannot be enclosed.**  
   No powerful company, state, locality, religious organization, or technical operator may turn water, food, health care, or energy into a tool of obedience.
3. **Dissent, non-participation, exit, and movement remain real.**  
   Leaving a community does not remove shelter, health care, food, safety, or basic rights. A person can return to the common floor without joining any community, move to another way of life, or later participate again.
4. **Harm cannot simply be exported.**  
   The costs of profit or comfort cannot be imposed unilaterally on other people, places, workers, ecosystems, animals, or future generations.
5. **Cross-boundary impacts require shared coordination.**  
   Watersheds, climate, logistics, infectious disease, waste, and safety are governed across the actual scope of their effects.
6. **Institutions remain stoppable, remediable, and revisable.**  
   Severe harm can be paused; survival is restored first; victims receive remedy; and institutions can be revised, reduced, divided, replaced, or ended.

These conditions are not an ideological compatibility test. Belief, expression, and voluntary practice remain protected. Yet no label—market, tradition, culture, security, or public interest—automatically entitles an institution to take away another person's survival or rights.

## 3. Three social models that could operate at the same time

These are simulations for testing the coexistence conditions, not finished institutional plans.

### Solarpunk — joining ecology and technology

People who want to combine ecological repair with new technology can use basic energy, water, materials, and communication from Vital Commons to cultivate an ecological settlement.

They may choose renewable energy, circular agriculture, shared workshops, sensors, and AI assistance without imposing them on every resident. Mining, waste, surveillance, and data burdens cannot simply be exported elsewhere. Routes without AI and skills for manual continuity remain available.

### Capitalism and free markets — choosing competition and growth

People seeking greater wealth, convenience, expression, or technical challenge can create companies, investment, prices, rewards, contracts, competition, and complementary currencies above the common floor.

Success can bring additional options. Employment, debt, contract, or competitive loss still cannot remove food, water, health care, shelter, or safety. Market winners cannot own Vital Commons, and competition rules, ecological burdens, and effects on labor remain open to review.

> Competition becomes closer to freedom  
> when losing does not remove life.

### Traditional and local communities — centering craft and continuity

People who value craft, local knowledge, ritual, care, farming, fishing, and intergenerational continuity can minimize AI and build communities centered on human relationships.

Communities can maintain distinct cultures and commitments without fixing people into roles by birth, gender, lineage, faith, or inherited duty. Dissent or exit does not remove Vital Commons, and newcomers are not excluded from basic survival. Tradition retains value without becoming power to confine people.

### Several ways of life may overlap within one person

No one must belong permanently to a single application.

A person may support local farming and care, run a company in a market, create within another cultural sphere, and step away from a community for a time. Nagi's pluralism does not divide society into sealed boxes. It also protects the several lives that can coexist within one person.

## 4. When social models conflict

Nagi OS does not promise a world without conflict. Land, resources, noise, landscape, labor, religion, technology, data, and ecological burdens will still produce disagreements.

The question is not which ideology ranks highest. The process instead asks:

1. What concrete resources, infrastructure, rights, burdens, and effects are involved—not how agreeable a person or belief appears?
2. If effects remain local, how much room can affected people and local self-government retain?
3. If effects cross boundaries through watersheds, ecosystems, supply networks, or rights violations, which wider public sphere includes everyone affected?
4. How are Vital Commons and basic rights kept running during the dispute?
5. Does severe and hard-to-reverse harm require a temporary pause with narrow scope and a time limit?
6. Are reasons, minority views, review dates, appeals, remedies, and termination conditions preserved?

Resonant Democracy does not exist to defeat and delete one side. It builds revisable boundaries that preserve difference without allowing one way of life to take another person's survival or domain.

## 5. Nagi OS is not value-neutral

Nagi refuses to prescribe one way of life, but it is not an empty platform that treats every practice as equally acceptable.

Human dignity and kindness, opportunities to create, and cultural continuity remain higher commitments. Holding survival hostage, suspending basic rights, blocking exit through violence or destitution, or imposing hard-to-reverse harm on others or nature cannot be justified merely by invoking culture, tradition, markets, public order, or security.

People remain free to hold, express, and voluntarily practice different beliefs. The object of limitation is not belief itself, but the point at which institutional practice becomes domination over another person's survival and freedom.

## 6. Not “nothing ever crashes,” but “failure does not take people down with it”

No institutional design can completely prevent war, violence, disaster, corruption, scarcity, or technical failure. Nagi OS does not guarantee that society will never crash.

Its aim is to keep the failure of one institution or community from simultaneously removing food, water, health care, shelter, safety, and rights from people beyond it. Vital infrastructure remains distributed, with alternate routes, reserves, human skill, and manual modes. When harm occurs, dangerous functions can be paused locally, survival restored first, victims remedied, and institutions revised.

Peace is therefore not the absence of disagreement. It is a structure that makes disagreement less likely to become total destruction of people's conditions of life.

## 7. What the metaphor cannot explain

An operating-system metaphor cannot fully represent histories of land, care and family relationships, bodies, violence, discrimination, feeling, religion, cultural continuity, or the pain of migration. A formal right of exit is insufficient without practical support for shelter, language, work, care, and relationships.

Nagi OS could itself become a new central power. Who interprets common rules, who may pause or remedy harm, and who pays the institutional costs remain questions for law, finance, resources, evidence, and international relations.

The metaphor is therefore a map for reading Nagi's existing chapters as one relationship, not a completed social blueprint. Nagi OS must itself remain non-owned, criticizable, divisible, revisable, and terminable.

## Conclusion — a floor from which answers can be chosen again

Nagi's hypothesis is that humanity may need not one final social philosophy, but conditions under which different social philosophies coexist without breaking people.

> Ask not which ideology will own the world,  
> but whether every person can live, leave, return, and choose again.

# Reading Nagi

Nagi includes a reference overview, a philosophical core, rights and safety principles, institutional proposals, cultural and technical chapters, practical supplements, and historical drafts. You do not need to read everything in file order.

The Japanese README and public home are the philosophical source of truth. The English edition is a maintained bridge. Where nuance differs, the Japanese reference edition prevails until the difference is discussed and repaired.

## Five minutes

As an entry point for exploring alternatives to capitalism and future society, read [Nagi as a Future Social Philosophy](future_social_philosophy.html).

It introduces the highest commitments, Non-Ownership, Resonance, Breathing, Vital Commons, Resonant Democracy, Institutional Immunity, AI boundaries, nearby fields, strong objections, and unresolved questions.

For how Nagi supports different social philosophies and ways of life without prescribing one final model, read [Nagi OS as a Metaphor](nagi_os.html).

If you already have a specific question, begin with the [English Glossary](glossary.html) or the Japanese [FAQ](../faq.html).

## Twenty minutes — the core

1. [Nagi Core](nagi_core.html) — highest commitments and centerless structures
2. [Nagi Declaration](declaration.html) — a short public declaration
3. [Vital Commons](vital_commons.html) — the central institutional proposal
4. [Compass and Resonant Democracy](compass_and_resonant_democracy.html) — political direction
5. [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html) — the floor against conformity and domination
6. [Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html) — boundaries around records and personal memory

## One hour — institutions and safety

Add the following to the twenty-minute path.

1. [Governance and Safety](governance_and_safety.html) — map of political, rights, safety, and AI chapters
2. [Institutional Design and Practice](institutional_design.html) — preserve value without fixing victory and inheritance into power
3. [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html) — keep coordinating systems from becoming domination
4. [Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html) — detect harm, pause damage, provide remedy, and end systems
5. [The State as Revisable Public Functions](state_and_public_spheres.html) — unbundle survival, rights, culture, safety, and coordination

hasPart.name: Institutionalizing Non-Ownership
hasPart.description: Nagi's approach to non-ownership: protect personal life and creative personhood while loosening monopolies over land, knowledge, culture, nature, and foundational technologies.
hasPart.text:
# Institutionalizing Non-Ownership

Nagi's Non-Ownership does not mean possessing nothing.

What it questions is the point at which land, knowledge, culture, foundational technologies, and similar shared conditions of life become powers through which a small number of people can dominate others.

## What is protected

Private life, homes, memories, everyday belongings, and the personal dimension of creative work are protected around the individual's choice and security.

## What is opened

Educational resources, cultural archives, public infrastructure, natural resources, and foundational technologies are moved away from monopoly and opened to paths of use and inheritance.

## Roles

The roles of use, care, inheritance, derivation, and circulation are distinguished, with responsibilities for explanation and care attached.

A steward is not a ruler. A steward temporarily takes responsibility for care and explanation, and prepares a condition in which something can be passed on.

> Non-Ownership exists to loosen structures in which one person having too much makes it impossible for others to breathe.

→ [Inheritance of Intellectual Property and Assets](property_and_ip.html)  
→ [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../non_ownership.html)

hasPart.name: Observe, Loosen, Connect
hasPart.description: Nagi's minimal practice method: do not rush to conclusion; observe conditions and effects, loosen fixed assumptions, and prepare conditions for the next relation or collaboration.
hasPart.text:
# Observe, Loosen, Connect

The smallest unit of practice in Nagi is to observe, loosen, and connect.

## Observe

Do not put evaluation or conclusion first. Look at what is happening, who is affected and how, and what remains unseen.

Observation is not surveillance or the inference of personality and emotion. Define a purpose, handle only the minimum necessary information, and protect private boundaries.

## Loosen

Separate assumptions, roles, conflicts, and habits of language that have become fixed. Do not reduce a problem to simple good and evil; handle facts, feelings, institutions, interests, and time as distinct dimensions.

When danger is urgent, secure safety first. Do not use “loosening” as a reason to delay support or responsibility.

## Connect

Do not force different things into sameness. Prepare the conditions in which another conversation or collaboration can become possible.

Do not presume that a relationship must continue. Protect the choices to keep distance, rest, or leave.

This sequence can be used in making work, organizational practice, technical design, dialogue, and record-keeping.

hasPart.description: A concise introduction to Nagi's world view: no state, market, company, or AI is the center; society arises from layered lives, memory, land, culture, relationships, and nature.
hasPart.text:
# The Philosophical Background of Nagi

Nagi does not place the state, the market, corporations, or AI at the center of the world.

The world emerges from layered lives, memory, land, culture, relationships, and nature. Institutions exist to listen to these layers, reduce domination, and preserve room for what can be handed on.

Non-Ownership loosens monopoly. Resonance allows people to relate without erasing difference. Breathing returns recovery and circulation to social life.

Nagi is not a completed answer. It is a compass for resisting the urge to fix the future too quickly.

→ [Nagi Core](nagi_core.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../philosophy.html)

hasPart.name: Play and Structure
hasPart.description: Nagi's account of creativity: play opens exploratory room, while structure carries possibility into forms that can be shared, criticized, maintained, and repaired.
hasPart.text:
# Play and Structure

Play and structure are not opposites.

Play is exploration that cannot be measured only by immediate usefulness. It is room for trying words and relations that have not yet been settled.

Structure exists to carry the possibilities that have been found into forms that can be shared with others, criticized later, and maintained.

1. Play opens possibility.
2. Structure makes selected possibilities shareable.
3. When structure becomes too rigid, play opens room again.

The systems that support creation should not punish exploration. They should make responsibility and judgment easier to see, and allow people who use a system to participate in its revision.

Play is not a reason to treat unpaid experimentation as natural. When the time, access, care, or compensation needed for exploration is concentrated among only some people, the structure itself must be reviewed.

hasPart.text:
# Inheritance of Intellectual Property and Assets

Nagi considers how culture can be passed to future generations while protecting both creative work and everyday life.

A creator's name, context, intention regarding alteration, and material security are protected. Opening a work does not mean erasing the voices of creators or communities so that it can be used freely.

## Principles of inheritance

- Respect a person's wishes during life and the agreement of those concerned.
- Make public, private, and time-limited publication available as choices.
- Widen routes for education, research, and preservation.
- Attach provenance and context to derivative use.
- When openness becomes extraction, prioritize suspension and review.

Large assets and cultural resources need not remain closed within private gain alone. They can be inherited as social trusts or commons.

> Inheritance is not fixing the past in place.  
> It is passing a person's or a community's breathing into the future without harming it.

hasPart.description: Nagi's method for developing a public philosophy that remains open to criticism and correction by distinguishing fact, interpretation, norm, proposal, metaphor, and unresolved question.
hasPart.text:
# How to Cultivate Public Thought
## — Opening beautiful language to criticism and correction

Nagi is a public philosophy, not for imposing conclusions, but for thinking together about a freer and safer society.

For that reason, it does not conflate facts, interpretations, norms, proposals, metaphors, and unresolved questions. When more than one of these appears in a chapter, headings, notes, sources, and conditions should make clear what kind of claim is being made.

## Six layers to distinguish

- **Fact**: Events, materials, institutions, and data that can be checked. State sources and the relevant date.
- **Interpretation**: A way of reading what facts may mean. Do not hide that other interpretations may exist.
- **Norm**: A value judgment about what should be protected. Do not present it as though it were a universal fact.
- **Proposal**: A possible institution, technology, or experiment. State assumptions, interests, alternatives, and what could happen if it fails.
- **Metaphor**: Words such as Breathing, Resonance, and Compass that help people see the world differently. Do not confuse them with exact technical specifications.
- **Unresolved question**: A matter whose answer is not yet known. Do not rush to present it as settled.

## Questions before publishing

- Who is being overlooked?
- Does beautiful language make responsibility or conflicting interests vague?
- Are words such as culture or resonance being used to rename inequality, extraction, or unpaid labor?
- When something fails, who bears what burden?
- Does publication increase understanding and verification, or does it remove someone's safety or context?

When AI is used for drafting, summarizing, translation, or research support, do not hide sources, limits, or unverified points. Treat AI-generated material as material for review, not as verified evidence in itself.

Publicness is not the quantity of exposure. It is an increase in criticizability, corrigibility, and accountability.

Private experience, health, family, intimate relationships, and information about people who have not chosen publication must not become evidence or content for a philosophy.

> Nagi is not a completed answer.  
> It grows by finding weaknesses, correcting them, and learning through experiments in writing, institutions, technology, and organization.

→ [Credit and Accountability](credit_and_accountability.html)  
→ [Nagi Experiments](experiment_v0.1.html)  
→ [Repair and Cultural Co-Growth](repair_and_co_growth.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../public_thought_method.html)

hasPart.name: Quiet Practice
hasPart.description: A practical method for bringing Nagi into everyday life, organizations, creative work, and technical design: observe, loosen, and connect without stopping another person's breath.
hasPart.text:
# Quiet Practice
## — Observe, loosen, connect

Nagi practice begins by making room in everyday dialogue and work.

Do not rush toward conclusions. Check reasons, respect another person's pace, allow thinking time in meetings, review roles and burdens, and use failure for the next repair rather than concealing it.

## 1. Observe

Do not put evaluation or conclusion first. Look at what is happening, who is affected and how, and what remains unseen.

Observation is not surveillance. Do not record more than needed; protect consent and private boundaries.

## 2. Loosen

Separate assumptions, roles, conflicts, and habits of language that have hardened.

Do not reduce a problem to simple good and evil. Treat facts, feelings, institutions, interests, and time as distinct dimensions. When danger is urgent, secure safety before analysis.

## 3. Connect

Do not force different things into sameness. Prepare the conditions in which another conversation or collaboration can become possible.

Do not compel the continuation of a relationship. Keep open the choices to remain silent, rest, leave, and return.

> Quiet practice does not mean lowering one's voice.  
> It is the skill of making change without stopping another person's breath.

→ [Observe, Loosen, Connect](observe_loosen_connect.html)  
→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [Repair and Cultural Co-Growth](repair_and_co_growth.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../quiet_praxis_current.html)
